placement.position_note: PARTY-LINE FRONTAGE, DERIVED FROM THE COMMITTED PLAT (T-0078). This building does not stand centred on a lot at a typology setback: it stands ON the north face of blk_south_water_wells, the block's South Water Street frontage, whose line and bearing are read from the block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json — the same committed geometry the lot grid and the corridor gate are derived from. Its front wall is 1.50 m back from that lot line, which is the closest line the plat module's own margin allows and is not a measurement of this frontage, and its east wall is fixed by 3.0 m west of carpenter_south_water_store, which stands proud of the platted line and so cannot share a wall with the row. The bearing is the face's own, so the front looks square at South Water Street. The run carries no lateral offset, because a shared party wall is one wall and cannot wander. WHAT IS INVENTED IS STILL EVERYTHING THAT MATTERS: that a building stood here at all, which building it was, and that these particular units stood shoulder to shoulder. What the 1834 South Water Street view supports is the TREATMENT — a continuous working row of party walls rather than detached cottages set back on grass. The treatment is what this placement takes from it, and a run standing on any other face of the town is borrowing it from that one street: the view draws a row, it does not place this row. Standing on a derived block face is not standing on a recovered lot, and the side lot lines this row crosses were always conjectural.

The block and lot are the only location on the page, they are ground platted in 1839 out of the garrison's reservation, and they place nobody in the town of 1835. frontage.why: T-0078, and the owner's standing ruling of 2026-08-18 with it: "there should be more and denser buildings. this is important." The reference he supplied for this reach — "South Water Street in 1834", the south bank of the Main Branch — shows a CONTINUOUS WORKING ROW: one-storey log and frame buildings shoulder to shoulder facing the river, the street between them and the grassy bank, two-storey frame stores anchoring its east end. This block's anonymous roofs stood seven metres back from that frontage, a full lot apart, each nudged off the line by its own lateral offset and — because the placement rule takes its bearing from the way into the lot — facing the block's interior rather than the river. That is the shape of a distribution across a block, not of a street. They now stand ON the frontage: the line, its bearing and the end they pack back from are read from the committed block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json, and this recipe authors no coordinate for any of them. The 1.5 m setback is not a measurement of this frontage — it is the closest line the plat module's own lot margin allows, adopted so the street wall is one wall. NO ROOF IS ADDED: the run carries exactly the roofs the schedule dealt this block's frontage lots, with every id, family and dimension the one it already had. What the view drives is the treatment — a row on its line, facing the water — never a coordinate, and the side lot lines the row crosses between its own units were conjectural in every record this generator has ever written.
